title: 13 charged over 'phantom workers' scheme involving false CPF declarations in work pass applications

 singapore 13 charged over 'phantom workers' scheme involving false CPF declarations in work pass applications
 The alleged false declarations were made to inflate their foreign worker quotas, MOM said 
 A total of 13 individuals, including 10 company directors, have been charged with false declaration offences in work pass applications. PHOTO: AsiaOne file PUBLISHED ON November 17, 2026 3:16 PM BY Sean Ler A total of 13 individuals, aged between 44 and 77, were on Oct 29 and Nov 17 charged for allegedly making false declarations in work pass applications involving Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions.
 In a statement issued on Tuesday (Nov 17), the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) said 10 company directors, two alleged "phantom workers", and one office manager were allegedly involved in arrangements to inflate foreign worker quotas by making CPF contributions to individuals who did not genuinely work for the companies.
 According to MOM, the alleged false declarations were made to inflate their companies' foreign worker quotas, which constitute an offence under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act.
 The six company directors and one office manager from five companies charged on Nov 17 are:
 Chen Rendang, 60, Singaporean director of He Zhan Construction
 Huang Canming, 60, Singaporean director of He Zhan Construction
 Ho Koon Kiang, 68, Singaporean director of Kian Hiap Construction
 Pha Kian Seng, 68, Singaporean director of Kian Hiap Construction
 Thomas Lee Teng Jeong, 67, Singaporean director of KAH Engineering (1986) and Kuan Aik Hong Construction
 Tng Kay Lim, 74, Singaporean director of Kay Lim Construction and Trading
 Tan Su Eng, 68, Singaporean office manager of Kay Lim Construction and Trading
 All seven individuals are accused of making false declarations in 20 work pass applications, except for KAH Engineering's Lee, who was handed two amalgamated charges for making false declarations in 32 work pass applications.
 MOM said that its investigations found that, in some cases, the company personnel had sourced family members and personal contacts to be registered as local employees and receive CPF contributions, although these individuals did not genuinely work for the companies.
 Earlier on Oct 29, four company directors, each overseeing two companies, were also charged for making false declarations for "phantom workers". 
 On the same day, two individuals, 63-year-old Singapore permanent resident Guan Qi and Singaporean Quek Lai Hin, 64, were each handed one charge of abetting the making of a false declaration in a work pass application.
 MOM said that they were allegedly phantom workers who received CPF contributions despite not being genuine employees of the companies involved.
 They allegedly aided their employers' false declarations intentionally, the ministry added.
 The four company directors are:
 Huang Rong, 55, Singaporean director of Dengda Construction and Hong Construction Information
 Jin Haihua, 49, Singaporean director of Hua An Construction and Hua An Development
 Yang Li, 44, Singaporean director of Mingda Construction and Trading, and de facto director of DYS Construction
 Zhao Xuebin, 57, Singaporean director of Crec Construction and Senda Construction 
 All four Singaporean directors charged on Oct 29 are each accused of making false declarations in 40 work pass applications.
 MOM said that it may also impose financial penalties on 21 other phantom workers linked to the cases.
 They had allegedly received CPF contributions despite not genuinely working for the companies, thereby committing the offence of abetting the companies in inflating their foreign worker quotas.
 The offence of making a false declaration carries a fine of up to $20,000, an imprisonment term of up to two years, or both.
 MOM reminded all employers and employment agencies that work pass fraud is a serious offence under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act. 
 The ministry also advised members of the public not to accept CPF contributions from employers they do not work for, as doing so may constitute abetment of false declaration offences or the inflation of foreign worker quotas.
